article_title: Incorporating Cognitive Load and Knowledge Transfer for Multi-Domain Knowledge Tracing
citation: Haotian Zhang, Shucun Wang, Jinze Wu, Liang Ding, Shuochen Liu, Zhenya Huang, Jing Sha, Shijin Wang, and Qi Liu. (2026). Incorporating Cognitive Load and Knowledge Transfer for Multi-Domain Knowledge Tracing. arXiv:2608.24005. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.24005
title: LT-MKT framework: joint modeling of cognitive load and knowledge transfer for multi-domain knowledge tracing
description: LT-MKT is a knowledge tracing framework for multi-domain learning scenarios that jointly models two factors the authors argue are overlooked by single-domain methods: cognitive load and knowledge transfer. It constructs a Multi-domain Hierarchical Graph with LLM-guided reasoning, models cognitive load via "question difficulty, domain transition, and domain coverage", updates knowledge states with a GRU, and applies intraGAT and interGAT layers for prerequisite-based within-domain and cross-domain semantic transfer, followed by state fusion and prediction.
requirements: A Multi-domain Hierarchical Graph constructed from question texts and associated concepts, using an LLM backbone for prompt-guided relation extraction
Student interaction sequences spanning multiple domains with response correctness labels
constraints: Prerequisite relations are constrained to satisfy the DAG property, avoiding circular dependencies in learning paths
Other cognitive-load factors beyond the three modeled are left for future work
target_learners: Students in multi-domain online learning scenarios, e.g., grades 7-12 academic domains and programming learners
target_learning_goals: Accurate prediction of students' future performance and dynamic knowledge state assessment across multiple domains
key_sources: Haotian Zhang, Shucun Wang, Jinze Wu, Liang Ding, Shuochen Liu, Zhenya Huang, Jing Sha, Shijin Wang, and Qi Liu. (2026). Incorporating Cognitive Load and Knowledge Transfer for Multi-Domain Knowledge Tracing. arXiv:2608.24005. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.24005

article_title: Learning to Argue Through Dialogue: a Review of Instructional Approaches
citation: Chrysi Rapanta & Mark K. Felton. (2022). Learning to Argue Through Dialogue: a Review of Instructional Approaches. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09637-2
title: Three dialogue goals for LTA: sensemaking, articulation, and deliberation
description: The review proposes a typology of epistemic dialogue goals enacted by students in LTA settings, extending Berland and Reiser's (2009) proposal. Sensemaking dialogues aim at making sense of what others say or a phenomenon; articulation focuses on articulating relationships between sources of evidence or coordinating theories with evidence; persuasion dialogues focus on arriving at consensus (deliberation) or proving one's position best. The authors write: "Examples of such dialogue goals are the ones proposed by Berland and Reiser ( 2009), namely: sensemaking, articulation, and persuasion". They prefer the term deliberation to persuasion to avoid the misconception that persuasion must be confrontational.
requirements: Sensemaking is treated as a starting point for any constructive dialogue; deliberation presupposes sensemaking and articulation as elements of the deliberative process
constraints: The authors note it is still not clear what a dialogue-goal typology in educational contexts should take into consideration as a 'goal'
target_learners: K-16 students in classroom dialogue settings
target_learning_goals: Sensemaking, articulation of evidence relations, and deliberative persuasion through dialogue
examples: Studies coded with deliberation as primary task include science students using critical dialogue to evaluate solutions to a socio-scientific problem and students in a historical debate through role-playing
key_sources: Chrysi Rapanta & Mark K. Felton. (2022). Learning to Argue Through Dialogue: a Review of Instructional Approaches. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09637-2

article_title: Long-term cognitive and neurophysiological effects of mental rotation training
citation: Linlin Dong, Yufeng Ke, Xiaodong Zhu, Shuang Liu & Dong Ming. (2025). Long-term cognitive and neurophysiological effects of mental rotation training. npj Science of Learning 10:16. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00309-2
title: LTP- and metaplasticity-based account of lasting mental rotation training effects
description: The article proposes that prolonged repetitive training fosters cognitive reorganization and long-term consolidation through synaptic plasticity. It states that "Long-term potentiation (LTP), a sustained enhancement of synapses driven by recent activity patterns, is a form of synaptic plasticity that underpins learning and memory processes," strengthened by repeated activation of relevant neural circuits during training. It further invokes metaplasticity — "the plasticity of synaptic plasticity" — whereby regular training increases the likelihood of synaptic strengthening, regulating and prolonging plasticity to explain continued improvements 20 days after training.
requirements: Repeated activation of relevant neural circuits over an extended training period
constraints: Proposed as a possible explanation, not directly tested in the study
target_learners: healthy college students undergoing cognitive training
target_learning_goals: spatial cognitive skill acquisition and retention
examples: The authors offer this mechanism to explain continued improvements in neurophysiological responses and behavioral performance observed 20 days after training.
key_sources: Linlin Dong, Yufeng Ke, Xiaodong Zhu, Shuang Liu & Dong Ming. (2025). Long-term cognitive and neurophysiological effects of mental rotation training. npj Science of Learning 10:16. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00309-2

article_title: The Effect of Peer Support on University Level Students' English Language Achievements
citation: İrfan Sarı, Nadir Çeliköz, Süleyman Ünal. (2017). The Effect of Peer Support on University Level Students’ English Language Achievements. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.8, No.1. https://www.iiste.org
title: Language Teacher Assistant (LTA) program with weekly-monitored booklets
description: The LTA program paired each advanced-level volunteer "Assistant" with one unsuccessful "Supported Student" for a semester of peer support in English. Experimental groups "keep their logs in LTA booklets in accordance with the supervi sion of the academic staff", and those logs were "chec ked in a weekly period by the class-teachers". Achievement was measured with the American Language Course Placement Test (ALCPT), a standardized 54-minute test whose reliability was 0.98 by Split-half and 0.96 by KR-20.
requirements: Assistants must follow advanced level English language classes (the stated volunteer criterion)
Weekly teacher checking of LTA booklet logs throughout the 15-week semester
constraints: The study population was all-male, "For the reason of being a military academy there were no female participants in the st udy"
target_learners: university-level English learners, both advanced (assistants) and low-achieving (supported) students
target_learning_goals: English language achievement as measured by the ALCPT
examples: 400 experimental students (200 Assistants, 200 Supported) monitored via LTA booklets over 15 weeks in the 2015-2016 fall semester, compared with 400 control students following traditional lessons
key_sources: İrfan Sarı, Nadir Çeliköz, Süleyman Ünal. (2017). The Effect of Peer Support on University Level Students’ English Language Achievements. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.8, No.1. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1131776

article_title: Supporting Teachers' and Students' Knowledge of Geometric Similarity
citation: Seago, N. (2013). Supporting Teachers' and Students' Knowledge of Geometric Similarity. Proceedings of the 35th annual meeting of the North American Chapter of the International Group for the Psychology of Mathematics Education. https://www.uic.edu
title: LTG Foundation Module: 30 hours of video-case-based professional development on geometric similarity
description: The Foundation Module is the central component of the Learning and Teaching Geometry PD materials, consisting of "10, 3-hour sessions that are intended to provide teachers with a thorough grounding in key mathematical and pedagogical issues related to similarity." Each session centers on unedited digital video clips of unstaged classrooms, chosen because they "typically represent a conceptual hurdle or portray some degree of mathematical confusion." The module follows a mathematical storyline moving from a transformational view of congruence and similarity through dilation properties to area and connections with slope and linearity.
requirements: A teacher educator facilitator using the materials with teachers in professional development settings
Carefully designed focus questions to guide viewing and analysis of the video clips
constraints: The finalized version had not been tested, nor had the complete package including four Extension Modules been used with any teacher group at the time of writing
target_learning_goals: Mathematical knowledge for teaching geometric similarity
Supporting students' understanding of similarity aligned with the Common Core State Standards
examples: Field tested in 8 U.S. sites over two academic years with 87 treatment and 40 comparison teachers recruited by nine facilitators
key_sources: Seago, N. (2013). Supporting Teachers' and Students' Knowledge of Geometric Similarity. Proceedings of the 35th annual meeting of the North American Chapter of the International Group for the Psychology of Mathematics Education. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED584497

article_title: Supporting Teachers' and Students' Knowledge of Geometric Similarity
citation: Seago, N. (2013). Supporting Teachers' and Students' Knowledge of Geometric Similarity. Proceedings of the 35th annual meeting of the North American Chapter of the International Group for the Psychology of Mathematics Education. https://www.uic.edu
title: LTG theoretical framework: professional learning as interactions among teacher educator, content, and teachers, adapted from Cohen, Raudenbush and Ball
description: The project's frame adapts Cohen, Raudenbush and Ball's framework in which "the content of the video case materials focus on the interactions between the teacher, the content (in this case, similarity tasks), and the students, within the context of an authentic classroom environment." The materials mirror this for professional learning: the teacher educator, the content of teaching and learning geometric similarity, and the participating teachers. "The LTG Study is based on the premise that both classroom learning and professional learning opportunities are a function of these reciprocal relationships."
requirements: Use by a teacher educator who faces a parallel set of relationships with the teachers they work with
target_learning_goals: Expanding mathematical knowledge for teaching geometric similarity
key_sources: Seago, N. (2013). Supporting Teachers' and Students' Knowledge of Geometric Similarity. Proceedings of the 35th annual meeting of the North American Chapter of the International Group for the Psychology of Mathematics Education. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED584497

article_title: Optimising the educational utility of live tissue training in trauma surgery.
citation: Swain Cara, Cohen Hugo, Routh Jennifer, Helgesson Gert, Rickard Rory, Karlgren Klas. (2025). Optimising the educational utility of live tissue training in trauma surgery. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07846-9
title: Three-phase framework for optimising live tissue training as a simulated learning event (Planning, Delivering, Experiencing)
description: The article organises participants' optimisation suggestions into three themes reflecting stages of participation in a simulated learning event: Planning (what LTT should be used to learn and for whom), Delivering (logistics, pedagogic methods, framing of the animal), and Experiencing (clinical realism, contextual realism, real-life survival). The authors map these onto Nestel and Gough's six-stage simulation design — "Our Planning theme is akin to the preparing stage, with the Experiencing theme reflective of the simulating stage" — and combine them with simulation theory and learning theory to generate recommendations.
requirements: Analysis grounded in interview data from learners and educators with prior LTT experience
constraints: Developed specifically for LTT in surgical trauma training; the authors note theme boundaries are not sharply delineated and sub-categories interact bi-directionally
target_learners: Postgraduate surgical trainees and surgeons attending trauma courses
target_learning_goals: Technical surgical skills such as haemorrhage control
Non-technical skills including team-working, decision-making and stress management
examples: The framework's five Planning categories are framed as questions an educator might consider when designing a simulated learning event, from why learners attend to who should be recruited as faculty
key_sources: Swain Cara, Cohen Hugo, Routh Jennifer, Helgesson Gert, Rickard Rory, Karlgren Klas. (2025). Optimising the educational utility of live tissue training in trauma surgery. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07846-9

article_title: "Learning, Thinking & Conveying" training with experiential learning in the emergency department for undergraduate nursing students: A quasi-experimental study.
citation: Li Y, Cheng S, Liu D, Jiang W. (2025). “Learning, Thinking & Conveying” training with experiential learning in the emergency department for undergraduate nursing students: A quasi-experimental study. Medicine 2025;104:28(e43231). https://doi.org/10.1097/MD.0000000000043231
title: Four-week "Learning, Thinking & Conveying" training program with experiential learning for emergency department rotations
description: A 4-week structured training program combining "Learning, Thinking & Conveying" steps with experiential learning, developed against hospital teaching requirements and emergency department clinical practice needs. "The program included 10 thematic medical records, covering emergency triage, sudden death, acute myocardial infarction, acute cerebral infarction, trauma, poisoning, and shock, with 3 randomly selected for each internship cycle." Each week follows the five steps, ending with teacher-guided bedside practice and a written reflection journal.
requirements: Teaching teacher guidance for group PPT production, nursing rounds and one-on-one bedside supervision
Thematic medical records aligned with emergency department clinical practice needs
constraints: Evaluated only over 4-week internship cycles in one tertiary care emergency department
target_learners: full-time undergraduate nursing students beginning clinical practice
examples: Week themes included sudden death with CPR demonstration, acute myocardial infarction with 12-lead and 18-lead electrocardiogram exercises, and severe trauma with limb bandaging and fixation practice.
key_sources: Li Y, Cheng S, Liu D, Jiang W. (2025). “Learning, Thinking & Conveying” training with experiential learning in the emergency department for undergraduate nursing students: A quasi-experimental study. Medicine 2025;104:28(e43231). https://doi.org/10.1097/MD.0000000000043231

article_title: Low-tech intraocular ophthalmic microsurgery simulation: A low-cost model for home use.
citation: Golash Vidushi, Kaur Simerdip, Naveed Hasan, Nanavaty Mayank A. (2021). Low-tech intraocular ophthalmic microsurgery simulation: A low-cost model for home use. Indian Journal of Ophthalmology. https://doi.org/10.4103/ijo.IJO_242_21
title: LTIOMS: a smartphone-based low-cost home simulation model for intraocular microsurgical skills
description: LTIOMS replaces the operating microscope with a smartphone balanced on a stack of books so the camera looks vertically down at the simulated surgical field, viewed on the phone screen. The authors propose "a smartphone-based, low-cost, low-tech model with corresponding exercises for intraocular simulation that can be used at home". It uses household materials (grape, boiled potato, lozenge packets, straw hoops, poppy seeds, orange peel) with basic surgical instruments, and is intended as an adjunct to patient-facing surgical training when simulation facilities are inaccessible.
requirements: A smartphone with video camera and torch illumination, a raised stand (the article uses books of 10.5 cm height), basic disposable surgical instruments, and household materials for the exercise surfaces
constraints: The article states the model "cannot replace simulation training models using microscopes, vegetables, and animal tissue with real instruments in a theater setting"
The article states "the hand-foot-eye coordination cannot be replicated in our model"
The article acknowledges "the exercises in our model are not mimicking ophthalmic surgery steps" and offers only low-fidelity dexterity practice
examples: An iPhone X on a 10.5 cm book stand with x2 zoom video is used over a lozenge-packet 'anterior chamber' secured with Blu Tack for the dexterity and capsulorhexis exercises
key_sources: Golash Vidushi, Kaur Simerdip, Naveed Hasan, Nanavaty Mayank A. (2021). Low-tech intraocular ophthalmic microsurgery simulation: A low-cost model for home use. Indian Journal of Ophthalmology. https://doi.org/10.4103/ijo.IJO_242_21
